passage: At nine in the evening, in a second-floor flat in Hyderabad, the argument started over the Wi-Fi password. Harsh's mother, Uma, had changed it because his marks had dipped. "You can't just control my life!" Harsh shouted. "I have three tests this week, I'm stressed out!" Uma's voice rose too. "Don't shout at me! You're being disrespectful!" Harsh slammed his door. Inside, he thought: she shouts because she likes being in charge; I shout because I'm under pressure. In the kitchen, Uma told his sister Jaya, "He shouts because he's become arrogant. I only raised my voice because I'm worried about his marks and I had a terrible day at the office." Jaya, who'd heard both sides, just kept chopping onions.

qa.q: Why had Uma changed the Wi-Fi password?
qa.a: Uma had changed it because Harsh's marks had dipped.

qa.q: Why does Harsh think his own shouting is different from his mother's?
qa.a: Harsh thinks he shouts because he's under pressure from three tests, but that Uma shouts because she likes being in charge.

qa.q: What could Harsh and Uma try once they have both calmed down?
qa.a: Each could say what their own day was like before discussing the password, so both sets of pressure become visible.

qa.q: How is Jaya's view different from Harsh's and Uma's?
qa.a: Jaya has heard both sides, so she can see that each explains their own shouting by stress and the other's by character.

grounding: A teenage son and his mother each excuse their own shouting by stress while reading the other's as arrogance or control.

passage:
"Rayan, it's eleven. Phone. Now."
"Ammi, I'm finishing the physics worksheet!"
"You said that an hour ago."
"Because you keep interrupting! Why are you always shouting?"
"I'm shouting? You're the one yelling!"
"I'm yelling because I've got a test tomorrow and I'm stressed! You're yelling because you want to control everything."
Afreen put her hand on the doorframe. "Control? I'm yelling because I'm tired and worried you'll be exhausted tomorrow. You're yelling because you've become rude, young man."
"I'm not rude, I'm stressed!"
"And I'm not controlling, I'm worried!"
They both stopped. The fan clicked overhead.
"So we're both saying the same thing," Rayan muttered.
Afreen almost smiled. "Finish the worksheet. Ten minutes."

qa.q: What time is it when Afreen asks for the phone?
qa.a: It's eleven.

qa.q: Why does Rayan believe his own yelling is justified?
qa.a: He feels the stress of tomorrow's test from the inside, so his yelling seems caused by pressure, while Ammi's seems to come from wanting control.

qa.q: What could Rayan and Afreen do earlier next time?
qa.a: They could agree on a phone time before the evening starts, and each say 'I'm stressed' or 'I'm worried' before voices rise.

qa.q: How does Afreen explain her own yelling?
qa.a: Afreen says she is yelling because she is tired and worried he'll be exhausted, not because she wants control.

grounding: A teenage son and his mother each blame their own shouting on stress or worry and the other's on control or rudeness.

passage: I'm Sachin, and last Sunday I had a huge fight with my father about the cricket academy. He said the fees were too much this year. I said, loudly, that he never supports anything I love. He said, louder, that I don't understand money. Then I shouted that he just likes saying no. Later, lying on my bed, I was sure I'd only shouted because I'd had a terrible week at school and the selection trials are close. And he'd shouted because he's controlling. My mother, Chandrika, came in and said something I keep thinking about: "Your father thinks you shouted because you're a spoilt boy, and that he shouted because the shop had a bad month." I hadn't known about the shop. He hadn't known about my week.

qa.q: Why did Sachin's father say no to the academy?
qa.a: He said the fees were too much this year.

qa.q: Why was Sachin so sure his own shouting was different?
qa.a: He knew about his terrible week and the close selection trials, so his anger felt explained, while his father's seemed like pure control.

qa.q: What could Sachin try in the next talk with his father?
qa.a: He could share how his week went and ask about the shop's bad month, so both of them see the other's pressure.

qa.q: How does Sachin's father see the same fight?
qa.a: His father thinks Sachin shouted because he is a spoilt boy, while his own shouting came from the shop's bad month.

grounding: A teenager explains his own shouting by a bad week but his father's by control, while the father sees it the opposite way.

passage:
Family counsellor's note, Wednesday. Joint session: Darshan, 15, and his father, Madhav.
Both arrived still angry about Sunday's argument over Darshan's phone at the dinner table. I asked each to describe it separately.
Darshan: "I shouted because I had two tests on Monday and I was stressed. Papa shouted because he always has to control everything."
Madhav: "I raised my voice because I'd had a terrible week at the shop and I was tired. Darshan shouted because he has no respect."
Each described their own shouting through their day and the other's through their character. When I read both answers aloud, there was a long silence. Madhav said, "I didn't know about the tests." Darshan said, "I didn't know about the shop."
What I did next: I asked each to write one sentence starting "Maybe you shouted because…" for next session. Both took the paper.

qa.q: What did Madhav say about his week at the shop?
qa.a: He said he'd had a terrible week at the shop and was tired.

qa.q: Why did each of them feel their own shouting was understandable but the other's was not?
qa.a: Each could feel their own stress, the tests or the tiring week, but only saw the other's raised voice, so the other's shouting seemed to come from control or disrespect.

qa.q: What task did the counsellor set for next session, and how might it help?
qa.a: Each will write a sentence starting 'Maybe you shouted because…', which pushes them to look for the other person's situation instead of only their character.

qa.q: What changed for Darshan and Madhav when the counsellor read both answers aloud?
qa.a: Hearing the other's situation for the first time, the tests and the shop, each seemed to see the other less as controlling or disrespectful and more as stressed too.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a teenage boy explaining his own shouting by stress and his father's by control, while the father sees it the other way round.

passage:
Sunday night
Another fight with Mummy. It started because I hadn't cleaned my room and she said "Vaibhav, look at this mess" in That Voice and I shouted "Leave me alone!" OK, I shouted. But I'm doing mock tests all week and I'm exhausted and nobody gets it. I'm not a shouty person, I'm just stressed.
She shouted back, which is typical. She loves being in control of every little thing. She can't just let anything be.
Then later I heard her on the phone with Masi, who probably thinks I'm a brat now. Mummy said, "I lose my temper only because I'm so worried about his exams. He shouts because he's become so rude."
So she thinks SHE is the stressed one and I'M the rude one. Which is literally the opposite.
Yamini, my mother, if you ever read this: I'm not rude. I'm tired.
Vaibhav

qa.q: What was Vaibhav's room like when the fight started?
qa.a: He hadn't cleaned his room, and Mummy called it a mess.

qa.q: Why does Vaibhav feel his shouting is stress but Mummy's is about control?
qa.a: He knows how exhausted the mock tests are making him, so his own shouting has a reason, but he doesn't see her worry, so her shouting seems to be about wanting control.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav try next time before deciding why Mummy is shouting?
qa.a: He could remember what he overheard on the phone and ask whether she is worried rather than controlling, and tell her about his tiredness calmly once they have both cooled down.

qa.q: How does Yamini seem to see the same argument?
qa.a: Yamini sees her own temper as coming from worry about his exams and sees Vaibhav's shouting as rudeness, the mirror image of how he sees it.

grounding: A teenage boy's diary shows him explaining his shouting as stress and his mother's as control, while she sees it exactly the other way round.

passage: At dinner in their Nairobi flat, Daniel's phone buzzed for the fifth time, and his mother, Wanjiru, reached over and turned it face down. "Not at the table." Daniel snapped. "You always have to control everything!" He stormed to his room and slammed the door. Lying on his bed, he told himself he hadn't really been shouting; he was just stressed about the chemistry test tomorrow and the group chat arguing about it. Mum, on the other hand, just liked being in charge. In the kitchen, Wanjiru scraped the plates, telling herself she hadn't really been angry. She was exhausted from a double shift at the hospital and just wanted one quiet meal. Daniel, obviously, had simply become rude. Neither of them knew about the other's day.

qa.q: What was Daniel stressed about?
qa.a: The chemistry test tomorrow and the group chat arguing about it.

qa.q: Why did Daniel feel his own snapping was different from his mother's?
qa.a: He felt stressed and saw his outburst as caused by the test, while he saw his mother's action as her wanting control.

qa.q: What small step could help Daniel and Wanjiru after the argument?
qa.a: Each could say what their day was like, the test and the double shift, before judging the other's character.

qa.q: How does Wanjiru see Daniel's shouting?
qa.a: Wanjiru sees it as Daniel becoming rude, not knowing about his test stress, while she excuses her own reaction as exhaustion.

grounding: A teenage boy explains his outburst as stress and his mother's as control, while she explains hers as tiredness and his as rudeness.

passage: On visiting day at the boarding school, Siddharth's father arrived with a tiffin of rajma and the report card already in his hand. Within five minutes they were shouting in a corner of the visitors' hall. "You're not even trying!" "You never listen!" Later, back in the dorm, Siddharth told his friend Eshaan, "I only shouted because I'm stressed. Exams, hostel food, no sleep. He shouted because he just wants to control me." Eshaan, who had watched from the next bench, said slowly, "Your dad left home at four in the morning to get here. He kept checking the bus timetable the whole time you talked." Siddharth paused. "He didn't say that." "You didn't tell him about the exams either," Eshaan said. "He probably thinks you're just being rude."

qa.q: What time did Siddharth's father leave home?
qa.a: At four in the morning.

qa.q: Why does Siddharth feel his own shouting was different from his father's?
qa.a: He feels it came from stress about exams, hostel food and no sleep, while his father's shouting seems to him like a wish to control.

qa.q: What could Siddharth do at the next visit?
qa.a: Tell his father about the exam stress and ask about the journey, so each understands the other's pressures.

qa.q: How might Siddharth's father see the argument?
qa.a: He probably thinks Siddharth was just being rude, not knowing about the stress, while his own shouting came from worry and a long, tiring journey.

grounding: At a boarding school visit, a teenage boy blames his own shouting on stress and his father's on control, missing his father's situation.

passage: Uma, can I tell you something? Last night I had the biggest fight with Papa. I'm Abhinav, the calm one, remember? Right. So I shouted. I admit it. But I shouted because I've had boards stress for three weeks, no sleep, two mock tests. Papa shouted because he wants to control everything, like which tuition, what time I'm home. That's how it felt. Then this morning I heard him talking to Ma in the kitchen. He said, "I only raised my voice because I'm worried about his marks and the office is killing me. But that boy just screams at me because he's angry at the world." Uma, he said the exact opposite of me. His shouting was stress, mine was attitude. I stood there holding my toothbrush. We're both saying the same thing about ourselves.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling standing there holding the toothbrush?

passage:
Monday. Thomas slammed his door so hard the calendar fell off. Mum had said no to the Goa trip with friends. "She just likes controlling me," he texted Yash. "I only yelled because I'm stressed about exams."
Wednesday. Yash was at their flat for maths. From the kitchen he heard Thomas's mum on the phone to someone: "I yelled back because I'm exhausted from double shifts. But Thomas, he just gets angry at everything these days." Yash pretended not to hear.
Saturday. Walking to cricket, Yash finally said it. "Your mum thinks she yelled because she's tired, and you yelled because you're angry." Thomas stopped. "That's backwards. I yelled because I'm stressed." "Yeah. And she thinks she yelled because she's tired." Thomas kicked a stone a long way. "So we both think we had reasons."

passage: Siddharth, beta, you slammed the door on your mother just now, and you think she's the only one who shouts. Let your Jasleen Dadi tell you a story. When I was sixteen in Amritsar, my own mother and I fought every single evening. I shouted because I was tired from school and scared about exams. She shouted, I was certain, because she wanted to rule my life. One night, after a fight about my hair, I found her little diary open on the sewing machine. I shouldn't have read it. I did. "Today I snapped at Jasleen because the grocer shouted at me and I had a fever. But she, she just has a temper now." Same fight. Same excuse. Only the names swapped. I closed it and sat on the stairs for an hour. That night I went back and said sorry first.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen Dadi find her mother's diary?
qa.a: Open on the sewing machine.

qa.q: What was young Jasleen feeling after reading the diary?
qa.a: She felt shaken and ashamed, seeing that her mother excused her own snapping with a bad day, just as Jasleen did, and blamed Jasleen's temper.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed things between them?
qa.a: Going back that same night to say sorry first, after seeing both of them had their own reasons.

qa.q: How did Jasleen's mother see the evening fights?
qa.a: She saw her own snapping as caused by fever and the grocer, but saw Jasleen's shouting as a new temper.

grounding: An elder recalls, as a teenager, blaming her mother's shouting on control and her own on stress, then reading her mother's diary saying the reverse.

passage:
The board exam was the next morning, the power had gone off in the Nagpur flat, and Madhav was trying to revise by torchlight when his mother, Urmila, came in for the third time. "Have you finished physics?"

"Stop checking on me!" he shouted.

She shouted back. "Don't speak to me like that!"

He slammed the book shut. In his head: I'm stressed, I have an exam, she's controlling me.

In the kitchen, Urmila leaned on the counter, shaking. In her head: I'm scared for him, the power's gone, he's being disrespectful.

Madhav came out an hour later for water. She was sitting in the dark.

"I shouted because I was stressed," he said.

"I shouted because I was worried," she said. "Not to control you."

He blinked. He had thought her shouting was just anger. She had thought his was just rudeness.

They sat together until the lights came back.

qa.q: Why was Madhav revising by torchlight?
qa.a: The power had gone off in the Nagpur flat.

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling, and how did he read his mother's shouting?
qa.a: Madhav felt stressed and saw his shouting as caused by the exam, while he read his mother's shouting as anger and control.

qa.q: What helped them understand each other?
qa.a: Each said out loud why they had shouted, which showed the other the situation behind it.

qa.q: How did Urmila see Madhav's shouting at first?
qa.a: Urmila saw it as disrespect, while feeling that her own shouting came from worry.

grounding: The night before an exam, a teenager explains his shouting as stress and his mother's as control, while she sees the opposite.

passage:
Imran's argument with his father started over the phone bill and ended with both of them shouting.

"You're always angry!" Imran yelled. "You just want to control everything!" He stormed out to the park.

His friend Dhruv found him on a bench. Imran vented: "I shouted because I'm stressed. Exams, cricket, everything. But Abbu shouts because he's just an angry person."

At home, his father was telling Imran's mother: "I'm tired from the shop, and worried about money. But Imran shouts because he's become rude and ungrateful."

Dhruv listened, then asked, "Does your dad have anything stressful going on?"

Imran paused. The shop had been losing customers. His father had been sleeping badly.

"Maybe," he said slowly. "But he should understand me."

"Maybe he thinks the same thing."

Imran stared at the ground. He had given himself all the reasons. He had given his father none.

qa.q: What did the argument start over?
qa.a: The phone bill.

qa.q: Why did Imran see his father as "just an angry person"?
qa.a: Imran felt angry and hurt, and explained his own shouting by stress while seeing his father's shouting as character.

qa.q: What did Dhruv ask that helped Imran rethink?
qa.a: Dhruv asked whether Imran's father had anything stressful going on, which made Imran notice the shop and the lost sleep.

qa.q: How does Imran's father see Imran's shouting?
qa.a: His father sees it as rudeness and ingratitude, while seeing his own shouting as caused by tiredness and worry.

grounding: A teenager explains his shouting as stress and his father's as anger, while the father thinks the opposite.

grounding: A teenager explains his shouting as stress and his father's as control, while the father sees the opposite.

passage: It was the Saturday before Diwali, and the whole flat was upside down for cleaning. I was on the sofa with my board-exam sample papers when Papa asked me, for the third time, to take down the curtains. I shouted, "Can't you see I'm studying? I'm so stressed!" He shouted back, and I stormed off. Later I texted Irfan: "My dad is so controlling. He just loves yelling." Irfan wrote back, "Didn't you yell first?" I typed, "That was different, I was under pressure." That night I heard Papa tell Mummy, "The boy has become so rude, Lalit never listens. And I'm only tense because the painters come on Monday." I lay awake thinking: he says I'm rude and he's tense. I say I'm tense and he's rude. We were both describing the same afternoon.

qa.q: Why did Lalit think his own shouting was fine but Papa's was controlling?
